HTSI
INTERVIEW
EXPERIENCE
Pankaj Khushalani
Third Year
Information Technology
Summer Internship 2022 
 Software Developer Role

TABLE OF
CONTENTS

The mid-sem had just gotten over and the internship drive resumed with PwC on
September 26, 2021, with their online test. Hours before PwC's online test, a new company
made its entry to the on-campus internship drive, which no one had ever heard of. In
comes Hilti Technology Solutions India Pvt. Ltd. based in Pune of the parent company - Hilti. 
Neither had anyone heard of Hilti nor HTSI. They didn't even have a website or a physical
office and were visiting any campus in India for the first time, with VJTI being their
beginning. We just knew that it is one of the few product-based companies that visit VJTI
and offer a great stipend of 80K per month. 
2 days later, when TPO sent out the October schedule, we were excited to see HTSI
announcing their online test on October 1 with interviews scheduled for the next day.  
I had no clue what to prepare in particular. There were absolutely no past experiences
found on this COC drive, GFG archives, or anywhere on Glassdoor. But I had no time to
research the company as I had my interviews for Fiserv on October 1. I was hoping for the
wee bit of luck to play its charm with Fiserv not announcing the results on the same day
and hence allowing me to sit for HTSI interviews. And that did happen, Fiserv didn't
announce their results till 4 days later and I stood a chance for HTSI.
After 2 interview rejections, not being shortlisted for interviews with 5 companies, I thought
the worst that could have happened, had happened. I only did what I could; do my
processes and wait for the results to follow. After attending the Hilti PPT scheduled on
October 1, 2021, I wanted to give my best for HTSI.
Disclaimer: If you are in a hurry, skip to article 3.
I wrote this experience as I would expect it from a senior - the
background, about the company, the interviews, the preparation.
01 PREFACE
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A

Platform: Microsoft Teams.
Attendees: All final and third-year students with CPI 6 or above from all branches.
The presentation was taken forward by the technical leads at HTSI and gave the students
an overview of Hilti, their products, what is HTSI, and the internship program.
About: Hilti is a multi-national company based in Liechtenstein that builds and markets
products used in manufacturing and construction works, which includes hardware,
services, and software - where HTSI came in. HTSI is the technology center for Hilti based
in Pune, India that works on developing one of their major products - ON!Track Asset
Management.
What I appreciated a lot about the presentation was the HTSI brought in their software
and HR team from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia who were going to shift to Pune to work onsite
next year. They also shared their experience of working at Hilti Malaysia.
02 THE PPT
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
Some details that were shared regarding the
internship program

03 ONLINE TEST
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
In order to implement the Windows screen switch shortcut (WIN + TAB), we need to
use a Most Recently Used (MRU) strategy which brings the recently accessed window
to the front. However, the question was quite long and many got confused while
perceiving the question. 
Given a list of numbers indicating the window number and a number indicating
the window number to be accessed, modify and return the list after applying
the MRU strategy.
1 Coding question.
Participants: All 290 third-year students who applied for HTSI were shortlisted for
the online test.
Platform: Mettl - audio, video, and screen proctored. 
Duration: 90 minutes.
Questions:
Example: 
    input list - [5, 2, 3, 4, 1], window number to be accessed - 2
     output list - [2, 5, 3, 4, 1] 
Here, as Google Chrome is being accessed at the moment, the next time we use
WIN + TAB, it will appear at the front of the list.
This was the easiest coding question I had solved in ages. I had to simply find the
number and put it in front of the list.
There were 10 test cases - 4 Basic, 4 Necessary, 2 Edge cases as listed on Mettl and I
passed all of them.
There were ample choices for the preferred programming language for the
question; I had used C++ 17.
There was a pool of questions and few students had slightly tougher questions.

H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
30 questions on Cognitive Ability (timed section - 30 minutes limit).
These were basic logical reasoning questions with 7-8 mathematical
reasoning questions towards the end. You can practice these on
indiabix.com.
This was the first section I had attempted and wanted to rush through it
thinking that the coding section would be tough given the length of the
question so I solved the last 4 questions haphazardly and submitted this
section.
6 questions on Data Structures.
These were some good questions on the usually asked interview questions
such as implementing stack with queue and vice versa, also on merge sort,
creating BST, and contiguous memory allocation of arrays.
I was able to solve all the questions but stack and queue questions took
some time to verify. 
5 questions on Database Management Systems.
Simple SQL queries and a really good question on the cardinality of
relationships of tables in a database.
6 questions on Networking.
Questions on the OSI model, transport layer were asked which are the most
commonly asked topics in interviews.
There was one question on IPv6 which I was not sure of.
7 questions on Object-Oriented Programming.
Questions on composition, aggregation were asked based on OOD.
Java questions were asked based on OOP.
6 questions on Operating Systems.
Questions were asked on deadlock, threads, thrashing and there was one
specific question on different methods that could be used to create a thread
in Java which I fortunately knew.
 
 
In a nutshell, all the sections were really easy. And from past experience, when the
test is easy, time becomes a deciding factor. Hence, I submitted the test with 17
minutes left on the timer.
The shortlist for the interview was declared the day after the online test on October
2 at 11 AM. Out of 290 students, only 30 were shortlisted for technical interviews that
were scheduled from the first slot being at 4 PM on the same day to 9:15 PM at
night being the last slot.

Technical Interview (40 minutes)
Situation - I and my peers had the objective of learning natural language processing and
knew quite a bit of supervised learning and wanted to make a project in the same. I was
the team lead and came up with the idea of predicting prices of cryptocurrencies using
sentiment analysis of tweets.
Task - We had to first acquire a dataset, study the techniques in various research papers
that prove the correlation between cryptocurrency prices and narrative economics (I
explained each term as I went on mentioning it). The project deliverables also needed to
be decided and since we were all familiar with Django, we decided to run our price
prediction model's backend on the same. Since live updates were decided to be shown on
the frontend with a visualization of a candle-bar plot, we decided to use ReactJS for the
frontend.
Action - Here I explained the workflow that was decided, the dataset used, and the prior
research that was referred to.
Finally, I mentioned the result which was the accuracy of the model with the visualization
of the prediction that was created, and all libraries and frameworks that were explored. 
My interview was scheduled for 5:30 PM. From the online test and the PPT, I had gotten a fair
idea that Java will be tested for sure along with DBMS. So, I revised OOP, multithreading, 2
design patterns in Java along with several SQL queries to prepare for the interview.
I joined the Microsoft Teams meeting at 5:28 PM and was cordially greeted by their HR from
Malaysia who was really sweet and with him was an engineer at HTSI. I was assigned to a 
 breakout room at 5:30 PM.
There were 2 interviewers, the female interviewer had her camera off throughout the
interview. They both greeted me and said they would introduce themselves first and I should
then proceed with mine. The male interviewer had his camera on and was smiling more than
me during my introduction.
The questions began with my resume. I was asked to explain my latest project, which was
CryptoFutureX. I was asked what was it all about and I made use of the STAR method (I had
seen seniors mentioning it everywhere but didn't see an example for the same so mentioned
it below).
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
04 INTERVIEW 1

Do you know what is cryptocurrency?
When did you first learn about blockchain?
Why did you go with the Sentiment140 dataset?
Did you use any database for your project?
Is the VJCoin blockchain you mentioned based on proof-of-work or proof-of-
stake?
You need to set a size for the array first before storing these words in it. How will
you get the size?
Why not use the set data structure?
What if the input is online (i.e., the input is a stream of characters), how will you
reverse them?
Do you know some method in Java that can make the work easy for you?
The cross-questions were : 
I had mentioned VJCoin which I had first seen in our canteen and that helped me gain
interest in the domain, but I was unable to answer the last question since I didn't know
its implementation.
Next, I was given a simple coding question - Find occurrences of 7 in all digits present
in the array.
Example - input = [7, 17, 20]; output = 2
I was asked to write the pseudocode for the same on a notepad. First I shared what I
understood about the question, posed the above example in front of them and asked
if this is correct and then proceeded to write the pseudocode and finally did a dry run
of 2 examples. They were pleased with the solution and didn't ask any other questions
on this.
The second coding question was the reverse all the words in a string where the words
are delimited by a period ('.'). This was again an easy one. I was given the example
'abc.def.xyz' which is to be reversed as 'xyz.def.abc'. Right away I gave the approach
that I will store all the characters in a word till a period is encountered and store the
string in an array. Then, I can reconstruct the string with the collected words. I was
interrupted and asked:
Here there was a discussion on the StringBuilder and String classes in Java. The use of
'split' method of String class. Then how I would do the same in Python (I think they
asked me in Python too because my pseudocode was 'pythonic'). Then I was also
asked about the mutability of strings in Java. 
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A

How had it been working with HTSI since its inception and that too working from
home?
What are the Hilti products that an intern will be exposed to?
They mentioned that they are only focusing on the ON!Track Asset
Management product which majorly uses Spring Boot.
 I was curious to know if they used Quarkus, which is faster than Spring Boot, as a
part of their platform to which the female interviewer laughed and said, "No dear,
it's the plain old JVM; it works fine for us."
Then came OOP and I was asked to explain polymorphism in Java. What is dynamic
vs. static binding in Java? How is polymorphism in Java different from C++?
Always explain OOP concepts with a real-life example.
Finally, I was given a schema of an Employee table and asked to find the 2nd highest
salary in as many ways as possible.
schema - Employee (EName, EId, Salary)
First, I cleared if the 2nd highest distinct salary was asked of just the 2nd highest and it
was the latter.
The first query I mentioned was finding the highest salary from a table that excludes
the highest salary.
The second query used the TOP clause in SQL where the female interviewer tried to
confuse me a lot regarding ordering the table twice but in the end, she was convinced
with my answer.
Finally, I asked the interviewers:
I was glad the interview ended on a good note. I thanked both of them and exit the
meeting. Then, I was told by the TPO CRs, who were coordinating with Hilti HR to be
ready for the next round as students were being called on a rolling basis. 
A thing I had noticed during the interview was that sometimes both interviewers had
their camera off and took some time in getting back with another question. Initially, I
thought that there were uninterested in the interview as it was evening and they were
working on Gandhi Jayanti but my friend told me they were probably adding remarks
for me after each question to submit to HR.  
16 students were shortlisted for the HR interview. My interview was scheduled for 6:20
PM and I wasn't told how long it would be.
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A

HR Interview (30 minutes)
What was the scholarship all about?
Were there other people in the program? Did you interact with them?
Tell me something about the people you met.
Yet again, I was greeted and congratulated by the HR guy from Hilti Malaysia as I
entered the meeting room and was sent to the breakout room. The interviewer had his
camera on for 2 minutes and told me to wait as he read my performance report.
He turned out to be from Hilti Malaysia and greeted me with a huge smile. He asked
me to introduce myself. As I began:
I am Pankaj Khushalani, currently in my third year of pursuing a B.Tech. in Information
Technology at VJTI, Mumbai. I am an avid learner and inquisitive about learning new
things (he nodded his head at this point and started listening more attentively). It was
this curiousity that led me to take up science after my school. Though I didn't have
computer science as a subject in 11th and 12th, I got acquainted with C programming
and later on learned C++ in 12th. Hence, I developed a fond interest in programming
and wanted to pursue the same (there was a big smile on his face and I was glad that
after all my interviews there was one interviewer who showed genuine interest). In my
2 years at VJTI, I have achieved a CGPA of 9.62 and have developed projects in
domains of web development using Django & ReactJS, Android mobile application
development using Kotlin, and machine learning. Last summer, I got the experience of
working on a machine learning model and embedded systems as an intern. This
summer, I learned about cloud native technologies with the  SUSE Cloud Native
Foundations Scholarship program (his eyes went wide open as he heard SUSE and
interrupted me).
He asked:
He was really interested in the bonding I had created with people around the world
during the program. Then he asked me to continue my introduction.
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
05 INTERVIEW 2

Could you share a bit on your role at Hilti?
How tough had it been for you to manage setting up the entire HTSI  team
remotely?
What projects of Hilti have you been exposed to?
Here we again had a good discussion on SAP HanaDB, how their team migrated
their database with no downtime, the work culture at Hilti, my experience with
HanaDB.
He explained the working of the database team in quite a detail.
Recently, I became the Cloud Computing Lead at Google Developer Students Club,
VJTI and I am also a Core Team Member of Community of Coders, VJTI.
I was interrupted again and asked about the role of these clubs at VJTI.
Then, as I was getting to the extra-curricular part of my introduction he asked,
"Pankaj, tell me what you do for fun." Instantly I said - "Chess". He started laughing
and fell back on his chair so hard that he disappeared into the virtual background he
was using. He said, "I don't know about chess so could you share something else that
you do for fun". After that episode, I had two options, either to have a long
conversation on my peculiar and outrageous taste in music or about the book I was
reading. I went with the latter.
I mentioned the book I was reading - Algorithms To Live By - and talked about the
algorithm I had come across which was the optimal stopping algorithm and the
interesting problem of serial monogamy. From this point, it was an extremely casual
conversation where he asked me - how do you assess love with logic, what are your
plans for marriage, why are most marriages in India arranged marriages, why are
some people siding with love now, do you think the optimal stopping algorithm is now
redundant - the conversation went in a flow and it was fun.
He asked me if I knew where Kuala Lumpur was and if I had been there. Then he asked
me if I had any questions.
Finally, I thanked him for the wonderful time and he was happy with the talk as well.
He told me that he wished to take the conversation further sometime in the future and
wished me good luck with the results.
It was indeed the best interview I had given. Then, I was eagerly looking forward to the
results.
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A

Around 5 PM on October 3, the list of the final selects was declared
and I was fortunate to be one of 8 selected for the Software
Developer Internship position at HTSI for the summer of 2022. 
The process didn't end there. We were instructed to join a final
meeting with the interviewing team at 5:30 PM. It was simply a
formality. The Software Delivery Lead, Product Lead of HTSI, and the
HR team from Hilti Malaysia were present in the meeting. They
congratulated us and asked us what we liked the most about the
process. They informed us how we would proceed from here regarding
the offer letter and a bit on the onboarding process.
We were asked to fill an anonymous feedback form for the entire
internship drive experience.  
I thank you if you have come this far in this document. I hope you have
learned something new that helps you out. This CoC archive is
something that I and my peers have religiously referred to and I am
glad that I get to contribute to it now.
Hope you put your best foot forward and luck be with you! 
Luck might take time to catch up but when you know the effort you
have put in, the processes will follow 😄
If you have any queries, feel free to contact me on LinkedIn or email
me at pankajkk218@gmail.com. Would be happy to help!
H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
06 CONCLUSION

H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
07 THE PREP
Data Structures & Algorithms
Had to unlearn and re-learn DSA in C++ in semester 4 by slowly and steadily
solving topic-wise data structures questions on GFG.
Began with 450dsa.com in March and to date solved 208 questions.
Tried out InterviewBit because everyone was doing it; not for me.
Switched to LeetCode in July to start with Top Interview Questions.
For DP, Stacks, Sliding Window (MUST), Heap - Aditya Verma.
For Graphs - take U forward.
Tips - 
Always revise the sorting algorithms, basic data structure questions
because they are frequently asked in interviews such as quick sort, merge
sort, stack using a queue, queue using stack, graph traversals, etc.
Make notes for each topic that you cover. These could be on some pattern
that you identified in such questions such as finding Kth order statistic in
an array being related to a heap or some syntax that you find tough to
remember such as the declaration of priority queue in C++.
Don't hit and trial by submitting your code; it just wastes time. Rather do a
dry run of example input and expected output. You won't be asking an
interviewer to confirm your code multiple times. so develop the habit of
verifying it twice and submitting it once.
Sometimes you may be asked to write the driver code, data structure
implementation along with the algorithm for the given question - in both
online tests and interviews. Do practice writing driver code for linked list,
tree, and graph questions.  
Object-Oriented Programming
Always referred to this article from Edureka for quick revision.
MUST DO - virtual functions (if you use C++), abstract classes vs. interfaces in
Java.
Do not ignore Java even if you don't use it as many companies use Java and
ask MCQs in their online test on Java. Study Java OOP from Javatpoint.
If you mention both C++ & Java in your resume, know their differences well.
For low-level design questions, refer to https://crack-oop-system-
design.herokuapp.com/.
Tips - 
Don't just study the concepts, implement them in code as well. You may be
asked to demonstrate these concepts in C++ or Java.
Always back your explanation of OOP concepts with a real-life exmaple.

H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A
Operating Systems
Religiously read Silberschatz-Galvin-Gagne. Later realized it was too much :)
Simply watch the entire OS playlist of Gate Smashers and make notes!
Can't go without GFG commonly asked questions.
Tips -
Virtual memory is extremely important along with process
synchronization techniques such as mutex locks, semaphores.
If you know Java, try to practice multithreading in Java.
Multitasking vs. multiprogramming, processor vs. core, parallelism vs.
concurrency, thread vs. process are common comparison questions so do
them well.  
Database Management Systems
Watched Sanchit Jain's playlist on DBMS.
If beginner, practice SQL on HackerRank and then move to LeetCode.
This covers all the important SQL queries.
For indexing, refer to Abdul Bari's video in particular.
Not much theory is asked except for ACID properties and normalization. For
other theory questions, refer to GFG interview questions.
Tips -
If you have used a database in any of your projects, be well prepared to
talk about the schema and queries done on the database. 
You should also be able to justify the choice of the database made for the
project.
Don't be worried about vendor-specific SQL clauses such as DENSE_RANK
while practicing SQL queries. There are hundreds of SQL clauses and you
are not supposed to know all.
Computer Networks
Study in brief about each layer of the OSI model, focus on network and
transport layers.
Study TCP, UDP, and the differences between them along with IP.
Only if you have enough time, go through IP addressing from Gate Smashers,
3.1 to 3.13.
Last Minute Notes on CN from GFG.
System Design (rarely asked, but I was asked a lot on it in my Fiserv interview
because of my experience in cloud)
If you are really new, refer to sudoCODE's playlist for a System Design Primer.
If you have prior exposure to some concepts of cloud, you can directly go to
Gaurav Sen's playlist. 
Rooting for you!! 🎉
